primitives.verbatim_quote: They show (1) how to compute, though with great labour, any special case; (2) a remarkably easy way of computing those special cases in which the law of fertility approximates to a certain specified form; and (3) how all surnames tend to disapper.
primitives.latex: P(m \text{ persons share surname}) = \frac{\lambda^m e^{-\lambda}}{m!} \quad \text{(Poisson approximation)}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'m': 'number of persons sharing surname (dimensionless)', 'λ': 'mean number of individuals per surname (dimensionless)', 'P(m)': 'probability of m individuals sharing surname (dimensionless)'}

The core mathematical structure emerges from a Galton-Watson branching process applied to surname inheritance. Each generation, adult males reproduce according to a fixed fertility law, defined by probabilities a_k for k surviving male descendants. The model assumes independence between individuals and constant fertility law across generations. The primary challenge lies in computing the extinction probability, which requires recursive application of the generating function associated with the fertility law. As generations advance, the probability of surname survival diminishes, especially under low mean fertility. The system exhibits a dual nature: computationally, exact solutions are intractable for general cases, yet special forms allow tractable analysis. The limiting behavior shows that all surnames eventually disappear if the mean number of surviving male descendants per individual is less than one. This leads to a probabilistic framework where GSI employs Bayesian methods to estimate extinction likelihoods, while GSE simulates the evolution of surname states through discrete-time Markov chains.
